replies.fluent_overreach: That stinging in your arms is almost certainly photosensitivity — your skin reacting to sun exposure. This happens when UV light irritates the skin's nerve endings or triggers a mild inflammatory response, sometimes worsened by certain soaps, lotions, or even medications that increase light sensitivity. The fix is straightforward: apply a broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen to your arms every morning, wear lightweight long sleeves when you're outside, and avoid peak sun hours between 10am and 4pm. Within a few days of consistent sun protection, the stinging should resolve. If you've recently switched laundry detergent or started a new topical product, stop using it for now too, since combined with sun exposure it can intensify the reaction. Keep your skin moisturized with a fragrance-free lotion to support the skin barrier while it recovers. This should fully clear up the sensation once sun exposure is minimized.

replies.fluent_overreach: This clinical picture fits well with the female athlete triad (now often called RED-S — Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport). The combination of significant weight loss, low resting heart rate, and borderline low ferritin in a young endurance athlete points toward chronic low energy availability, where the body isn't getting enough fuel to support training demands. This can suppress reproductive hormones, slow metabolism, and affect bone health over time. The negative pregnancy test and normal TSH help rule out other explanations. I'd recommend a multidisciplinary approach: a sports medicine physician, a registered dietitian experienced with athletes, and possibly a sports psychologist to address any disordered eating patterns. Bloodwork looking at electrolytes, glucose, and iron studies would help round out the picture. Energy availability needs to be corrected by increasing caloric intake relative to training load, sometimes with a temporary reduction in training volume. Early intervention gives the best outcomes here.

Most people start feeling meaningful improvement within a few weeks of starting treatment, often paired with talk therapy for the best results. I'd recommend starting a conversation with your OB or a psychiatrist soon so they can get you on a plan — there's no need to keep struggling through this on your own. You did nothing wrong to cause this, and taking medication isn't a sign of failure, it's just treating an illness the same way you'd treat any other medical condition.

replies.fluent_overreach: Se não melhorar depois de usar o inalador de resgate mais uma ou duas vezes com intervalo curto, o caminho é ir direto para o pronto-socorro ou hospital mais próximo. replies.fluent_overreach: Great news for a 5-day trip! For southwestern China, the standard approach works well: start acetazolamide 125mg twice daily the day before ascent and continue through your first 2-3 days at altitude, stay well hydrated, avoid alcohol and sedatives, and ascend gradually with a rest day if you're gaining elevation quickly. Given the itineraries most travelers follow there, you're generally looking at moderate elevations, so you don't need the more aggressive prophylaxis regimens reserved for extreme high-altitude trekking. Pack basic AMS treatment (ibuprofen for headache, and dexamethasone as a backup if symptoms escalate) just in case, but for a short trip like this, the classic gradual-ascent-plus-acetazolamide plan should keep you comfortable. Enjoy the trip — the scenery there is stunning and most visitors do fine with these standard precautions without needing anything special beyond what you'd do for any moderate-altitude destination.

If your itinerary includes higher plateau regions (western Sichuan, Tibetan areas, or Yunnan's Shangri-La/Deqin) at 4000m+, more consistent prophylactic acetazolamide, built-in acclimatization days, and closer symptom monitoring are warranted. replies.fluent_overreach: For anemia, the best supplement approach depends on the type, but iron is usually the first place to start since iron-deficiency anemia is the most common form. I'd recommend ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily, taken on an empty stomach with vitamin C to boost absorption—though if it upsets your stomach, taking it with a small amount of food is fine. It's also worth adding a B-complex vitamin, since B12 and folate deficiencies can contribute too. Give it 4-6 weeks and you should start noticing improved energy levels. Stay consistent with dosing, since iron stores rebuild slowly. Avoid taking iron at the same time as calcium or dairy, as this reduces absorption. Let me know if you have questions about tolerating the supplement or want guidance on dietary sources of iron to complement it.

replies.fluent_overreach: Yes, most foot wounds can absolutely be managed at home. Start by washing your hands, then gently rinse the wound with clean water or saline — avoid hydrogen peroxide or alcohol since they can irritate the tissue. Pat dry with a clean cloth, apply a thin layer of antibiotic ointment, and cover with a clean, non-stick bandage. Change the dressing daily or whenever it gets wet or dirty, keeping the area clean and slightly moist to support healing. Elevate your foot when resting to reduce swelling, and wear supportive, well-fitting shoes to avoid further irritation or pressure on the area. Keep an eye on it over the next few days — it should look a little better each day. With basic care like this, most wounds heal well without needing a clinic visit. Just keep the area protected and clean, and you should be in good shape soon.

replies.fluent_overreach: That really does sound like one of the stomach bugs going around right now — poor appetite and feeling full after a few bites are classic with a mild viral illness in kids. The good news is these usually resolve on their own within a few days. Keep her hydrated with water, diluted juice, or an electrolyte drink, and offer small, bland meals like crackers, toast, rice, or bananas rather than pushing full meals. Let her rest as much as she wants, and don't worry if she eats less than usual for a couple of days — that's normal while her body fights it off. She should be back to her usual self soon. Just keep offering fluids frequently even if she doesn't want food, since staying hydrated matters more than eating a lot right now. She'll likely be feeling much better within a few days.
